Countries and partners have agreed new measures to advance implementation of the Global Framework on Chemicals at the first International Conference that took place in Geneva this week.
This includes an initial set of global indicators to help track progress towards its targets, two global implementation programmes to strengthen national legal and institutional systems and coordinated action across sectors and value chains, and an extension of the Global Framework on Chemicals Fund to support continued implementation in developing countries and countries with economies in transition.
Three years after the Framework was adopted in Bonn in 2023, the Conference focused on strengthening the foundations for implementation. With most of its 28 targets due by 2030, the decisions taken in Geneva provide a basis for better tracking progress, identifying gaps, accelerating action and continuing financial support for implementation.
More than 1,200 participants took part in the Conference, representing governments, civil society and non-governmental organizations, the private sector, international organizations, academia and other stakeholder groups.
Chemicals are involved in around 95 per cent of manufactured goods, while the global chemical industry contributes an estimated US$5.7 trillion to global GDP and supports approximately 120 million jobs – this makes chemicals management an economy-wide issue, with implications across production, supply chains, product design and waste.
“There is no time to lose between now and 2030. The decisions taken in Geneva give countries and stakeholders a stronger basis for measuring progress, identifying where gaps remain and directing support where it is most needed,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of the UN Environment Programme (UNEP). “What matters now is quickly translating these commitments into real action that delivers safer chemistry, cleaner production, healthier workplaces and economies that protect people and planet.”
The Conference provisionally adopted an initial set of indicators to begin tracking progress towards selected targets of the Framework and also agreed to continue developing the Framework’s measurability structure including advancing the work on the two high-level indicators covering the global burden of disease and the global environmental burden attributable to chemicals and waste. The Secretariat will develop an accessible online reporting tool and prepare an assessment of progress ahead of the second International Conference.

The Conference also adopted two global implementation programmes to support delivery of the Framework’s targets. The first programme focuses on strengthening legal frameworks and institutional capacities for the sound management of chemicals and waste. The second focuses on industry engagement and action along value chains, with initial sector programmes covering construction, electronics, healthcare and textiles. Together, they provide a structure for governments, industry and other stakeholders to coordinate activities, share knowledge and strengthen implementation across countries and sectors.
The Conference also welcomed new guidelines to support national focal points in coordinating implementation of the Framework, as well as a capacity-building strategy to help countries and stakeholders identify capacity strengths, gaps and priority needs.
The Conference also agreed to continue work on existing issues of concern under the Framework, including chemicals in products, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, environmentally persistent pharmaceutical pollutants, hazardous substances within the life cycle of electrical and electronic products, highly hazardous pesticides, lead in paint, nanotechnologies and manufactured nanomaterials and managing per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).
The Conference also agreed to further develop the operational arrangements of the Global Alliance on Highly Hazardous Pesticides at the second International Conference.
The Conference also extended the duration of the Global Framework on Chemicals Fund , allowing it to receive voluntary contributions until 31 December 2033 and disburse resources until 31 December 2035. The Fund supports implementation of the Framework in developing countries and countries with economies in transition, and the Conference recognized its role in helping advance the Framework’s objectives.
The Conference also approved the indicative programme of work, budget and staffing structure for the Secretariat and the Fund for 2027–2029 and called for broader partnerships and additional voluntary financial and in-kind support for implementation.
“The value of this Framework will ultimately be measured by what happens for the better in countries, workplaces, supply chains and communities,” said Ms. Magdalena Frydrych of Poland, President of the first International Conference of the Global Framework on Chemicals. “This conference has energized our commitments, forged new partnerships, and provided a greater understanding of our challenges. Our task now is to build on these outcomes to meet the targets and achieve our vision.”
The Conference also convened a High-Level Dialogue under the theme “Together for a Better Future by Design”, bringing together ministers and senior leaders from government, business, finance and civil society. Discussions focused on improving chemicals transparency across value chains, scaling up safer alternatives through green and sustainable chemistry, and mobilizing investment, while emphasizing the urgency of taking action to address the challenges and opportunities associated with the safe and sustainable management of chemicals and waste.
During the Conference, UN Environment Programme and the World Health Organization also launched the 2026 State of the Science of Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals (EDCs) , the first major global update on EDCs science since the 2012 UNEP–WHO assessment, with a companion UNEP synthesis, From Evidence to Action: Addressing Endocrine-Disrupting Chemicals Across Sectors , that translates the science into suggested practical actions for policymakers across food packaging, cosmetics, toys, textiles, healthcare, agriculture, pharmaceuticals, waste, and other sectors.
Progress will be reviewed at the second International Conference, to be hosted by the Republic of Malta in 2029. The Conference also elected Marcus Richards of the Saint Vincent and the Grenadines as President of the Bureau for the next intersessional period.
The Global Framework on Chemicals (GFC) is a voluntary multistakeholder and multisectoral international framework that supports countries and stakeholders in developing and implementing solutions for the safe and sustainable management of chemicals and waste. It is coordinated by the GFC Secretariat, hosted under the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) . The GFC Fund is the dedicated financial mechanism established to support implementation of the framework, providing catalytic financing to help countries and stakeholders turn its objectives and targets into action on the ground. Across its first two funding rounds, the Fund has committed approximately US$8.2 million to 13 national and regional projects supporting 23 countries.
The UN Environment Programme is the leading global voice on the environment. It provides leadership and encourages partnership in caring for the environment by inspiring, informing and enabling nations and peoples to improve their quality of life without compromising that of future generations.
